title: Plan Multi-Paragraph Outlines
outcome: Plan short keyword outlines with distinct paragraph jobs, plausible order and task coverage; choose three or four roles according to need, not a fixed essay template.

teaching.lesson1: An outline decides which ideas belong where before drafting. It is not a place to write the entire essay.
teaching.lesson2: Compare paragraph jobs and find repetition, but do not treat three/four paragraphs as a universal rule.

demo.prompt: Write a short message to the public library suggesting an afternoon skills-sharing session. Explain who could take part and give two practical arrangements.

steps.label: Notice
steps.text: Topic: skills-sharing afternoon; Task: suggest and explain; Must include participants and two arrangements; Boundary: short message to public library.

steps.label: Choose a path
steps.text: Start with the proposal, then let organizers picture how it works.

steps.label: Keyword role notes
steps.text: P1: proposal; free skills-sharing; community. P2: volunteer demonstrations; tables; sign-up. P3: teenagers and adults; beginner slots; invite feedback.

steps.label: Why roles differ
steps.text: P1 says WHAT; P2 details practical HOW; P3 identifies WHO and a closing request.

steps.label: Reject duplicate roles
steps.text: Repeating that the event is nice adds no distinct reader job. Replace repetition with a missing participant/arrangement.

steps.label: Transfer principle
steps.text: Two paragraphs might also work for a short email; adapt outline to audience, not an exact four-paragraph rule.

teaching.a1: Optional icons/roles: What? How? Who? English keyword notes are enough; no full essay needed.
teaching.b1: Compare a proposal with a public notice and explain why their reader jobs may differ.

cycleA.prompt: A community group plans a one-day food-waste reduction event. Write a short proposal to neighborhood volunteers: explain the event, the food-sharing activity, and how participants will handle leftover items safely.

strip.task: Propose a practical plan for neighborhood volunteers.
strip.mustInclude: Event, sharing activity, safe leftover handling.
strip.boundary: Volunteers/community; one day; safe practical actions.

labels: P3: Safe next steps and close

cards.text: Opening: one-day food-waste event; volunteers invited
Food-sharing station: label unopened shelf-stable food; clear collection area
cards.rationale: Describes a central practical action without a food-safety guarantee.

cards.text: Leftover handling: follow organizers' safety guidance; contact suitable charities before donating
cards.key: P3: Safe next steps and close
cards.rationale: Handles leftovers cautiously, not assuming donations are automatically accepted.

cards.text: All paragraphs: the food event is nice and good
cards.rationale: Empty praise does not create distinct roles.

cards.text: Change the color of city buses
P2: food-sharing station; P3: food-sharing station, no new action
cards.rationale: Repeats one paragraph's reader job with no new action.

cycleA.repairPrompt: Rewrite one repeated role into a new action that makes the event proposal more useful. Do not imply that food donation is automatically permitted.
cycleA.whyPrompt: Explain why your repaired role has a different job from the other roles.

cycleB.prompt: A community youth center is preparing a weekend makers' fair. Write a proposal that explains (1) what the fair would offer, (2) two different activity areas, and (3) how visitors can participate safely. Plan the paragraph jobs using short notes before drafting.

strip.topic: Weekend makers' fair at a community youth center.
strip.task: Propose and explain an event to organizers.
strip.mustInclude: Fair purpose; TWO distinct activity areas; safe participation arrangement.
strip.boundary: Youth center; weekend visitors; practical/safe activities; outline only.

cycleB.instruction: Pick three or four paragraph roles. Give each role a reader job and keyword/short-phrase notes; usually 3–8 notes per role, but this is guidance, not a semantic quality cutoff. Explain the order and whether any jobs overlap. Do not write a full essay or force a separate conclusion.
cycleB.a1: Optional roles: introduce / show / invite. A straightforward three-part plan is fine.
cycleB.b1: Compare a proposal vs public notice; optionally compress to two parts for a different short notice and explain.

transfer.prompt: An animal shelter wants a short letter suggesting a community donation drive. Plan a clear letter that explains the purpose, how people could participate, and what they should check before bringing supplies. Produce only a keyword outline.
transfer.instruction: Make a new 3- or 4-role keyword outline and explain how it covers the shelter's needs. Do not invent an official accepted-items list; suggest confirming with the shelter first.

supplemental.title: Outline versus full draft
supplemental.prompt: Plan a short community-garden volunteer invitation.
supplemental.question: Which entry is most suitable as an outline note?

options.text: Dear neighbors, I am writing with great excitement about a wonderful plan ... [full paragraph].
options.rationale: Prewrites a whole paragraph instead of a flexible note.

options.text: P1: invite volunteers; Saturday morning; community garden
options.rationale: Compact keywords capture one reader job and details.
Connector list without actual task content.
Word target isn't a content plan.

supplemental.title: Distinct paragraph jobs
supplemental.prompt: Outline a neighborhood tree-planting invitation: tell people when, what to bring, and why it helps.
supplemental.question: Which pair has the clearest distinct jobs?

options.text: P1: say planting is nice; P2: say planting is very nice
options.rationale: Repeats praise rather than new functions.

options.text: P1: explain when and where to join; P2: explain needed supplies and purpose
options.rationale: Splits logistics and preparation/benefit and covers the task.

options.text: P1: list famous footballers; P2: list football scores
P1: mention the same date; P2: repeat the same date with no new action
options.rationale: Duplicates a job, omitting other required information.

supplemental.title: Cover required parts
supplemental.prompt: Invite residents to a bike-safety talk. Include the place, starting time, and one planned practical activity.
supplemental.question: Which outline covers all required information without drafting the complete invitation?

options.text: Place; time; practical demonstration; audience: residents
options.rationale: Lists every requirement in planning notes.

options.text: I love bicycles; bicycles are excellent

supplemental.title: Flexible structure
supplemental.prompt: A short message to a club leader explains a simple event proposal and two arrangements.
supplemental.question: Which planning principle best fits?

options.text: Every response must have exactly five paragraphs.
options.rationale: Short message may not need long essay structure.

options.text: All paragraph roles must repeat the same proposal sentence.
Choose a small number of distinct roles that cover the task, even if opening and closing share one paragraph.
options.rationale: Flexible task-driven structure preserves required functions.

options.text: Skip required arrangements if they do not fit your favorite format.
options.rationale: Flexible structure does not permit omitting required details.

aiLens: Review whether each planned paragraph has a distinct reader job and covers the fair purpose, two activity areas and safe participation. Accept coherent 3-role or 4-role structures. Quote actual learner notes, do not draft a finished proposal.
